The land grant from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates (Genesis 15:18-21) is unconditional and eternal (Genesis 17:8). Israel has never possessed all of it permanently, so it awaits a literal fulfilment in the millennium (Amos 9:14-15).

The Davidic kingdom was offered to Israel by Jesus, rejected, and postponed. It will be set up on earth when Christ returns, with Christ ruling from Jerusalem over a restored Israel and the nations, and with a rebuilt millennial temple (Ezekiel 40-48).

Most classic dispensationalists see the 1948 return as a significant step in God's prophetic program, often linked to a regathering in unbelief that comes before spiritual renewal (Ezekiel 37:7-10). Leading writers such as John Walvoord treated it as a sign of the approaching end, though careful scholars avoid setting dates.
Romans 11:26 means a future national salvation of ethnic Israel at the second coming, after the tribulation, when the nation looks on the one they pierced (Zechariah 12:10).
Christian Zionism

Christian Zionism is a theological and political movement, not one academic school. It holds that God's covenant with Abraham gives the Jewish people a continuing right to the land, and that Christians should support the return of Jews to it and, today, the State of Israel. Its roots lie in English Puritan and evangelical hopes, in figures such as Lord Shaftesbury and William Hechler (an ally of Theodor Herzl), and in William Blackstone's 1891 memorial to the U.S. president. Since 1967 it has grown into a large movement, with organisations such as Christians United for Israel (founded 2006).

Israel means the Jewish people as an ethnic and national people. Many Christian Zionists are dispensational, but some, such as Gerald McDermott's 'new Christian Zionism' (2016), argue from Scripture and church history without a full dispensational system.

The land promise is permanent and still belongs to the Jewish people by divine gift (Genesis 17:8; Psalms 105:8-11). The return of Jews to the land in the twentieth century is seen as the hand of God.
Views on the kingdom differ, but most expect a future earthly kingdom centred on Jerusalem. Some focus less on end-time schemes and more on the present duty to bless Israel.

The modern state is widely seen as a fulfilment, or at least a providential sign, of prophecies of return (Isaiah 66:8; Ezekiel 37:21-22). Supporting it is often read as obeying 'I will bless those who bless you' (Genesis 12:3). Critics, including many Palestinian Christians, say this confuses a modern political state with biblical Israel; proponents answer that God's faithfulness to the Jewish people includes the land.
Romans 11:26 means a future salvation of the Jewish nation. Romans 11:28-29 is used to show that God's election of the Jewish people still stands, even in unbelief.
Israel: the Israel of God
Christ the true Israel

The fulfilment reading starts here: Jesus sums up Israel in himself. He is the Son, the Servant and the Vine, and the promises reach others only through him. Future-for-Israel scholars accept much of this typology but deny that it removes a future for the nation.
Called out of Egypt
Matthew applies Hosea's words about the nation to the child Jesus, so that Israel's story becomes his story.
The Servant named Israel
The Servant is called 'Israel', yet he also restores Israel and is a light to the nations (Isaiah 49:5-6).
The true vine
Israel was God's vine that gave bad fruit (Isaiah 5:7); Jesus calls himself the true vine and his disciples the branches.
All promises are Yes in him
Paul says every promise of God finds its 'Yes' in Christ.
The seed of Abraham
God promised Abraham a seed through whom all nations would be blessed. Paul reads 'seed' as pointing to one person, Christ, and then to all who belong to Christ.
The promise to Abraham
Abraham's seed will possess the gate of his enemies, and in his seed all nations will be blessed.
Seed, singular
Paul notes that the promise says 'seed', not 'seeds', and identifies the seed as Christ.
Heirs in Christ
Those who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise.
Children of the promise
Not the children of the flesh but the children of the promise are counted as the seed.

Canaan was promised to Abraham and given under Joshua. The New Testament widens the inheritance to the world and the new creation; the future camp holds that Canaan itself will still be given to national Israel.
Promised to Abraham
God promised the land of Canaan to Abraham and his seed as an everlasting possession.
Given under Joshua
The Lord gave Israel all the land he had sworn to their fathers.
Heir of the world
The promise to Abraham was that he would be heir of the world.
The meek inherit the earth
Jesus widens Psalms 37:11 from the land to the earth.
The temple

The tabernacle and temple were God's dwelling among Israel. In the New Testament, Christ's body and then his people are the temple; Revelation's new Jerusalem has no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple.
His body the temple
Jesus spoke of the temple of his body, to be raised in three days.
The church a holy temple
Jews and Gentiles together are built into a holy temple in the Lord.
A copy and shadow
The earthly sanctuary was a copy and shadow of the heavenly one.
No temple in the city
The Lord God and the Lamb are the temple of the new Jerusalem.
Jerusalem and Zion
Zion was the city of David and of the temple. The prophets promised that the nations would stream to it. Hebrews and Galatians speak of a heavenly Jerusalem to which believers have already come.
Nations stream to Zion
In the last days the nations come to the mountain of the Lord to learn his ways.
You have come to Mount Zion
Jerusalem above
The Jerusalem above is free and is the mother of believers.
The new Jerusalem
The holy city comes down out of heaven from God as a bride.
The throne of David

God promised David a son whose throne would last forever. The apostles preached that Jesus was raised and enthroned to fulfil this promise; dispensationalists traditionally place his reign on David's throne in a future earthly kingdom.
The covenant with David
God promised to raise up David's offspring and establish his throne forever.
Given the throne of David
Gabriel says God will give Jesus the throne of his father David, and his kingdom will have no end.
Raised to sit on the throne
Peter says David foresaw that God would raise the Christ to sit on his throne.
At the right hand
Peter cites Psalms 110:1: the risen Jesus is made Lord and Christ.
The people of God (ekklesia)
Israel was the 'assembly' of the Lord. The New Testament uses Israel's titles for the church of Jews and Gentiles; dispensationalists hold that the church shares these titles without becoming Israel.
God called Israel his treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.
Titles given to the church
Peter gives Israel's titles to scattered believers who were once 'not a people'.
One new man
Christ made Jew and Gentile into one new man, making peace.
One olive tree
Gentiles are grafted into the one olive tree among the natural branches.
The new covenant

Jeremiah promised a new covenant with the house of Israel and Judah. Jesus inaugurated it in his blood, and Hebrews applies it to the church. The future camp agrees the church shares in it now but expects a national fulfilment for Israel.
Promised to Israel and Judah
God promised a new covenant with the law written on the heart and sins forgiven.
The cup of the covenant
Jesus calls the cup the new covenant in his blood.
Applied to the church
Hebrews quotes Jeremiah at length and says the first covenant is now obsolete.
Ministers of a new covenant
Paul calls the apostles ministers of a new covenant of the Spirit.
God called Israel his firstborn son and demanded that Pharaoh let his son go.
At his baptism the Father calls Jesus his beloved Son, the one in whom he is pleased.
God called his son Israel out of Egypt in the exodus.
The child Jesus goes down into Egypt and returns, and Matthew says this fulfils Hosea's words.
Israel passed through the sea on dry ground; Paul calls this a baptism into Moses (1 Corinthians 10:1-2).
Jesus passes through the waters of the Jordan in baptism and the Spirit descends on him.
Israel was tested forty years in the wilderness to show what was in its heart, and often failed.
Jesus is tested forty days in the wilderness and answers each temptation with words from Deuteronomy (8:3; 6:16; 6:13), succeeding where Israel failed.
Moses went up Mount Sinai and brought God's law down to the people.
Jesus goes up on a mountain and teaches the law with his own authority: 'but I say to you'.
Israel was made up of twelve tribes descended from the sons of Jacob.
Jesus chooses twelve apostles, a sign of Israel reconstituted around himself (compare Matthew 19:28).
Israel was the Lord's vineyard, planted with choice vines, but it produced wild grapes.
Jesus says he is the true vine and his Father is the gardener; fruit comes by abiding in him.
God calls his Servant 'Israel, in whom I will be glorified', and gives him a mission to Israel and the nations.
Matthew applies the Servant song of Isaiah 42 to Jesus, the chosen one in whom God delights.
The glory of the Lord filled Solomon's temple, God's dwelling among his people.
Jesus calls his body the temple, to be destroyed and raised in three days.
God promised to set over his scattered flock one shepherd, his servant David.
Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep.
God fed Israel with manna, bread from heaven, in the wilderness.
Jesus says he is the bread of life, the true bread come down from heaven.
Water flowed from the struck rock to give Israel drink; Paul says 'the rock was Christ' (1 Corinthians 10:4).
Jesus cries out that whoever is thirsty should come to him and drink, and rivers of living water will flow.
Moses lifted up a bronze serpent, and those bitten who looked to it lived.
Jesus says the Son of Man must be lifted up in the same way, so that all who believe may have eternal life.
Israel was spared when God saw the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorposts.
Paul says Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed.
Jacob, who became Israel, saw a ladder joining heaven and earth with angels going up and down.
Jesus says his disciples will see angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man; he is the meeting place of heaven and earth.
Hosea pictures Israel, torn and struck down, being raised up on the third day; the prophets used death and resurrection for exile and return (Ezekiel 37:12).
Christ died for our sins and was raised on the third day 'according to the Scriptures', bearing Israel's exile and leading the true return.
The call of Abraham: a great nation and a blessing for all families

God tells Abram to leave his country and go to a land God will show him. God promises to make him a great nation, to bless him, to make his name great, and to make him a blessing. God will bless those who bless him and curse the one who treats him with contempt, and in him all the families of the earth will be blessed. The promise has three strands from the start: a people, a land, and a blessing that reaches every nation.
The call joins a nation, a land and a worldwide blessing. The blessing for 'all the families of the earth' answers the scattering of the nations in Genesis 11.
At the descent into Egypt God repeats that he will make Jacob's family a great nation there. By Exodus 1:7 the family has multiplied and filled the land of Goshen.

Paul says Scripture 'preached the gospel beforehand' to Abraham when it said that all nations would be blessed in him. The blessing is justification by faith, given to the nations in Christ (Galatians 3:14).
Peter tells the people of Jerusalem that they are heirs of the covenant with Abraham. God raised his Servant and sent him to them first, to bless them by turning each one from wickedness.
Abraham is 'the father of us all', Jew and Gentile who share his faith. Paul reads Genesis 17:5, 'father of many nations', as fulfilled in a believing family drawn from every people.
John sees a multitude no one can count, from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing before the throne. This is the 'all families of the earth' of Genesis 12:3 at the end of the story.

Genesis places Abram's call after his family moved from Ur of the Chaldeans to Harran (Genesis 11:31-12:4), when he was seventy-five years old. Most conservative scholars place the patriarchs in the early second millennium BC (Middle Bronze Age), though the dating is disputed and some critical scholars doubt the narratives are historical at all. K. A. Kitchen argues that details such as treaty forms, personal names and slave prices fit the early second millennium. The first certain mention of 'Israel' as a people in Canaan outside the Bible is the Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BC). By the time of the New Testament, Jewish teaching saw Abraham as the father of the nation and the model proselyte, which is why Paul's claim about 'the children of Abraham' (Galatians 3:7) was so sharp.

A Gentile believer is not a guest in someone else's family story. Paul says that those who are of faith are sons of Abraham and are blessed with him (Galatians 3:7-9). The promise that began with one man leaving his country now includes every believer from every nation, and the mission of the church is the way 'all families' are being reached.

Dispensational writers such as Walvoord, Pentecost and Fruchtenbaum agree that the blessing of the nations flows through Christ. But they hold that the Abrahamic covenant has distinct strands, and that Gentiles share in the spiritual blessing strand without taking over the national strand. The 'great nation' remains the physical descendants of Abraham through Isaac and Jacob (Genesis 17:19-21; 28:13-14). Christian Zionists add that Genesis 12:3 ('I will bless those who bless you') still applies to the Jewish people and so shapes how nations should treat them today.

Fulfilment writers such as O. Palmer Robertson and Gentry and Wellum answer that Paul does not divide the promise into separate national and spiritual parts. He says the promise was spoken to Abraham 'and to his seed', which is Christ (Galatians 3:16), and that all who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed and heirs (Galatians 3:29). The blessing-and-curse clause was spoken first to Abraham himself, then passed to Jacob (Genesis 27:29) and to Israel as God's people (Numbers 24:9); in the New Testament the people who carry that blessing are those united to the Messiah. They add that physical descent alone never made one a child of the promise (Romans 9:6-8).

Vlach and Saucy reply that Galatians 3 is about how Gentiles are saved, not about the future of the nation. Gentiles become Abraham's children by faith without becoming Israel, just as Genesis 12:3 itself distinguishes Abraham's nation from 'all the families' who are blessed through it. Paul still says that the promises 'belong' to his kinsmen according to the flesh (Romans 9:4) and that God's calling of them is irrevocable (Romans 11:28-29).
The land given to Abraham's seed, from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates

After Lot leaves, God tells Abram to look in every direction: all the land he can see will be given to him and his seed forever (Genesis 13:14-17). In Genesis 15 God binds himself by covenant. He passes alone between the cut animals as a smoking fire pot and a burning torch, and promises the land 'from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates', the land of ten named peoples.

God promises Abram all the land he can see, to him and to his seed forever, and a seed as many as the dust of the earth. Abram is told to walk through the land, but he owns none of it in his lifetime.
God alone passes between the pieces, binding himself to the promise. The borders run from 'the river of Egypt' to the Euphrates.
Under Solomon, the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt bring tribute and serve him. The Genesis 15 borders are reached in the form of a ruled empire.
Paul says the promise to Abraham and his seed was that he would be 'heir of the world'. The promise of Canaan is read as a pledge of the whole earth.
Abraham lived in the promised land as a foreigner, in tents. He looked for a city with foundations whose builder is God, and the patriarchs desired 'a better country, that is, a heavenly one'.
The promise ends in a new heaven and a new earth, where God dwells with his people. The 'land' has widened to the renewed creation (Matthew 5:5).

The covenant ritual of Genesis 15 matches ancient Near Eastern oath rites in which parties walked between halved animals, calling the same fate on themselves if they broke faith. Jeremiah 34:18-19 describes the same rite, and eighth-century BC Aramaic treaties from Sefire contain similar curse formulas. 'The river of Egypt' (Hebrew nahar) is read by some as the Nile's eastern branch and by others as the Wadi el-Arish, the 'brook of Egypt' of Numbers 34:5; this is disputed. The northern border at the Euphrates was reached only under David and Solomon (2 Samuel 8:3; 1 Kings 4:21, 24), and then as an area of vassal states rather than settled tribal land. The extent of the united monarchy is itself debated by archaeologists (the 'low chronology' of Israel Finkelstein against the views of Amihai Mazar and others).

The promise shows that God's salvation is not only for souls but for a place: God means his people to live with him in a real, good earth. Believers today are heirs of that promise, but like Abraham they live as strangers and pilgrims, waiting for the renewed earth (1 Peter 1:4; 2 Peter 3:13). Jesus' word that the meek will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5, echoing Psalms 37:11) is the same promise in its widest form.

Classic dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost, Ryrie) argue that an unconditional covenant, ratified by God alone, guarantees the land to Abraham's physical descendants in the exact borders of Genesis 15:18. Since Israel has never held all of this land permanently as its own possession, they hold the promise awaits the millennial kingdom (Ezekiel 47:13-48:29). Progressive dispensationalists such as Blaising, Bock and Saucy agree that the land will finally widen to the whole earth, but insist the widening includes, rather than replaces, the particular land of Israel.

Fulfilment writers answer that the Old Testament itself already widens the land. Psalms 2:8 gives the Messiah 'the ends of the earth' as his possession, and Psalms 72:8 sets his rule 'from sea to sea'. Robertson, Martin and Burge argue that Paul's 'heir of the world' (Romans 4:13) and Hebrews 11 show how the apostles understood the land: as a type of the renewed creation. The final inheritance is therefore larger than Canaan, not smaller, and it belongs to all who are in Christ. W. D. Davies notes that the New Testament almost never repeats the promise of Canaan as such, and instead attaches the holiness of place to the person of Jesus.

Vlach replies that 'widening' can still include the original land: the whole earth includes Canaan, just as the nations are blessed without Israel ceasing to be a nation. Saucy points to the New Testament's own hopes centred on Jerusalem (Luke 21:24; Acts 1:6-7), and Kaiser notes that God tied the land to the word 'forever' (Genesis 13:15). They argue that the silence of the New Testament on the land is an argument from silence and does not cancel explicit Old Testament oaths.
An everlasting covenant: God to Abraham's seed, and Canaan an everlasting possession

God confirms his covenant with Abraham and his seed after him as an everlasting covenant: he will be their God. He will give Abraham and his seed all the land of Canaan, where he is now a foreigner, as an everlasting possession. Circumcision is given as the sign of the covenant in the flesh (Genesis 17:10-14).
The covenant formula 'I will be their God' is joined to land 'for an everlasting possession'. Circumcision marks the covenant people.
At the exodus God recalls the covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He promises to take Israel as his people, be their God, and bring them into the land he swore to give.
Paul notes that the promises were spoken to Abraham and 'to his seed', singular, 'which is Christ'. Christ is the true heir of the everlasting covenant.
If you belong to Christ, you are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise. Circumcision of the heart, not of the flesh, now marks the covenant people (Romans 2:28-29; Colossians 2:11).
A loud voice says that God's dwelling is with people and that he will be their God and they will be his people. The covenant formula of Genesis 17:7 reaches its final form.

The word translated 'everlasting' (Hebrew 'olam) is used in the Law for other institutions that the New Testament treats as ended or transformed in Christ: circumcision as an 'everlasting covenant' in the flesh (Genesis 17:13), the Passover as a statute 'forever' (Exodus 12:14), and the Aaronic priesthood as an 'everlasting priesthood' (Exodus 40:15; Numbers 25:13). Israel lost the land twice for long periods: the north to Assyria in 722 BC and Judah to Babylon in 586 BC. After AD 135 (the Bar Kokhba revolt), Jews were barred from Jerusalem, renamed Aelia Capitolina by Hadrian. The question of what 'everlasting possession' means is therefore pressed by history as well as by exegesis.

The heart of the covenant is not real estate but relationship: 'I will be your God'. Believers in Christ share that covenant fully and will see it completed when God lives with his people forever. The same God who kept the promise to Abraham will keep his word to every believer.

Dispensationalists argue that 'everlasting' must mean what it says. Ryrie and Walvoord hold that because the covenant is unconditional and everlasting, physical Israel must possess Canaan forever, and the millennium and the eternal state will see that. Fruchtenbaum adds that Paul's 'seed' argument in Galatians 3:16 concerns the line of salvation, while Genesis also uses 'seed' collectively for the nation (Genesis 17:8 itself), so both senses stand.

Fulfilment writers such as Robertson, Waltke and Holwerda reply that 'olam often means 'for the whole age of this covenant' and is used of things (circumcision, the Aaronic priesthood) that Hebrews 7:12 and Galatians 5:2-6 treat as fulfilled. The 'everlasting possession' is not lost but transposed: Canaan was the type of the everlasting inheritance, which is the renewed earth. In this reading, the promise is kept more fully, not cancelled, because believers will possess the whole earth forever (Romans 4:13; Revelation 21:1-7).

Dispensational and premillennial writers (Horner, Vlach) answer that if 'everlasting' can be stretched so far, the eternal life promised to believers could be stretched too. They argue the right comparison is with God's promises, not with Mosaic rites, and that Jeremiah 31:35-37 ties Israel's survival as a nation to the fixed order of sun and moon. They also note that Genesis 17:8 names a particular land, 'all the land of Canaan', which is hard to read as a symbol.
A seed like the stars and the sand, possessing the gate of its enemies

After Abraham offers Isaac on Mount Moriah, God swears by himself that he will greatly bless Abraham and multiply his seed as the stars of heaven and the sand on the seashore. His seed will possess the gate of his enemies, and in his seed all the nations of the earth will be blessed, because Abraham obeyed God's voice.
God swears an oath by himself. The promise of countless offspring is joined to victory over enemies and blessing for all nations 'in your seed'.
In Solomon's day Judah and Israel are 'as many as the sand by the sea', eating, drinking and rejoicing. Deuteronomy 1:10 had already said Israel was as the stars of heaven in number.
The 'seed' in whom the nations are blessed is Christ. Isaac, the offered and returned son (Hebrews 11:17-19), foreshadows the Son who is offered and raised.
All who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed. The countless offspring of the promise now includes Gentile believers (Romans 4:16-18).
The final multitude from every nation that no one can number fulfils the 'stars' and 'sand' in their widest sense. Hebrews 6:13-18 treats this oath as the anchor of Christian hope.

2 Chronicles 3:1 identifies Mount Moriah, the place of Isaac's binding, with the hill where Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. Jewish tradition (the Aqedah) made Isaac's binding a central theme of atonement and faith. By the census figures of Numbers 1 and 26 and the summary of 1 Kings 4:20, the Old Testament itself records that the promise of number was fulfilled in national form by the united monarchy. Yet after 586 BC only a remnant returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:64 counts 42,360 in the assembly), so the prophets looked ahead to a greater multiplication (Isaiah 54:1-3).

Hebrews 6:13-20 says God swore by himself to Abraham so that those who flee to him for refuge might have strong encouragement. Every believer, Jew or Gentile, is part of the fulfilment of this oath. The growth of the church among all nations is God keeping his word to Abraham.

Dispensational writers accept that Christ is the singular seed and that believers are spiritual seed. But Fruchtenbaum and Walvoord distinguish three senses of 'seed': the natural seed (all physical descendants), the spiritual seed within Israel (believing Jews), and the spiritual Gentile seed. Gentiles share the blessing but are never called 'Israel' in their reading. The national promise of number and victory over enemies will be seen when Israel as a nation is restored and saved (Romans 11:26).

Fulfilment writers answer that Paul does not keep a separate national seed in Galatians 3. He moves from the many (Abraham's offspring) to the one (Christ) and back to the many (all in Christ), as N. T. Wright stresses in The Climax of the Covenant. The 'gate of enemies' is seen in Christ's victory over death and the powers (Colossians 2:15) and the church's advance against the gates of Hades (Matthew 16:18). Ethnic Israel is not excluded: believing Jews are the first members of this seed (Romans 11:1-5).

Dispensationalists answer that recognising believing Gentiles as Abraham's seed does not require saying the nation has no future. Romans 11 speaks of Israel 'according to the flesh' after Christ came, as 'beloved for the sake of the fathers' (Romans 11:28). In their reading the threefold seed makes better sense of all the uses of the word than a single spiritual sense does.
A treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation

At Sinai God tells Israel that if they obey his voice and keep his covenant, they will be his treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is his. They will be to him a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The promise has a condition ('if you obey') and a purpose: Israel is to stand between God and the nations as a priest stands between God and the people.
Israel is called to be God's treasured people, a priestly kingdom and holy nation, on the condition of keeping the covenant.
The covenant is ratified with blood sprinkled on the people. Israel's national life under the Law serves as the pattern of a holy people.
Jesus gives the cup as 'the new covenant in my blood'. The covenant people is now formed around the Messiah's own blood, not the blood of Sinai.
Peter gives the church Israel's titles: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession. He adds Hosea's words: once not a people, now God's people.
The Lamb has ransomed people from every tribe and nation and made them a kingdom and priests to God, and they will reign on the earth.

Exodus 19:1 dates the arrival at Sinai to the third month after the exodus. The covenant has the shape of an ancient Near Eastern vassal treaty: the history of what the great king has done (Exodus 20:2), stipulations, and blessings and curses (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28); scholars such as George Mendenhall and K. A. Kitchen compared it with Hittite treaties of the late second millennium BC, though the closest parallel is disputed. The date of the exodus is also disputed (a fifteenth-century date from 1 Kings 6:1, or a thirteenth-century date). Israel's history in Kings and Chronicles is largely the story of failure to keep this covenant, ending in exile.

Every believer is a priest: able to draw near to God through Christ and called to make God known to others (1 Peter 2:5, 9). The church does not have a priestly caste between God and the people; the whole people is priestly. The holiness once marked by food laws and the temple is now marked by lives that 'proclaim the excellencies' of God.

Dispensationalists note that Peter writes to 'exiles of the dispersion' (1 Peter 1:1), which some, such as Fruchtenbaum, take as mainly Jewish believers. More broadly, Saucy and Vlach argue that Peter applies Israel's titles to the church by analogy, without saying the church has become Israel. They point to Isaiah 61:6, where Israel will be called 'priests of the LORD' while the nations serve them, and to Zechariah 8:23, where people from the nations take hold of a Jew's robe; this, they say, describes a future national priestly role.

Fulfilment writers (Robertson, Beale, Hoekema) answer that Peter's language is not loose analogy. He gathers Exodus 19:6, Isaiah 43:20-21 and Hosea 2:23 and applies them to a mixed church, many of whom were Gentiles 'formerly not a people' (1 Peter 2:10; compare 1:14, 18 and 4:3 on their pagan past). Jesus had warned that the kingdom would be taken from the leaders of Israel and given to 'a nation producing its fruits' (Matthew 21:43). Revelation 1:6 and 5:10 then apply the same Exodus title to the whole redeemed people.

Future-camp writers reply that Matthew 21:43 is addressed to the chief priests and Pharisees (Matthew 21:45), so it transfers stewardship from Israel's leaders, not from the nation forever. Revelation 5:10 says the redeemed will reign 'on the earth', which premillennialists of all kinds read as pointing to an earthly kingdom after Christ returns.
